title: Every Big Movie Still Coming in 2026 — The Complete List
excerpt: Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday, The Batman Part II and more. Every major film still ahead in 2026, and which ones actually matter.
author: StarScoop Daily Staff
imageAlt: Avengers Doomsday backdrop — biggest movies still coming in 2026
metaDescription: Every big movie still coming in 2026 — Dune Part Three, Avengers Doomsday, The Batman Part II, The Odyssey and Wicked: For Good.
content:
2026 has one of the densest release slates in years — and most of the biggest films are still ahead.

Here's what's actually coming, what's confirmed versus reported, and which of these genuinely matter rather than just being large.

Avengers: Doomsday — December 18

The one with the firmest date. Robert Downey Jr. returns to the MCU as Doctor Doom — not as Iron Man — with the Russo Brothers directing.

Why it matters: this is the payoff film for everything Marvel has built since Endgame. The Multiverse Saga has been criticized for incoherence, and Doomsday is where it either pulls together or doesn't.

Reports of legacy Fox X-Men cast returning have driven most of the conversation. Treat specific names as reported until Marvel confirms them — we cover what's actually been said.

Full details: cast and release date guide · India booking guide

Dune: Part Three

Denis Villeneuve closes the trilogy, with Timothée Chalamet's Paul Atreides now Emperor and presiding over a holy war he spent two films trying to prevent.

Why it matters: this is the film the whole trilogy was built for. Frank Herbert's story was always a warning about charismatic leaders, and Part Three is where that argument has to land. It's an unusually difficult thing for a blockbuster to attempt.

No firm date confirmed. Villeneuve does not rush post-production, and the studio has protected his windows before.

Full details: everything we know · where to watch the first two

The Batman Part II

Robert Pattinson and Matt Reeves return, with Colin Farrell's Penguin and a Gotham left flooded and broken at the end of the first film.

Why it matters: the first film worked because it was a detective story rather than a superhero one, and it committed completely. Whether the sequel resists the pull to go bigger is the interesting question.

No confirmed date. The delay has been long — industry shutdowns, a DC leadership restructure, and Reeves writing slowly.

Full details: everything we know

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey

Matt Damon as Odysseus, with Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson and Charlize Theron.

Why it matters: Nolan following an Oscar sweep by adapting a three-thousand-year-old poem is the least predictable move available to him. Homer's fractured, non-chronological structure also happens to suit exactly how Nolan builds films.

Full details: cast and plot breakdown

Wicked: For Good

Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande return for the darker second half, where the friendship at the center fractures.

Why it matters: the first film proved a stage musical could work at this scale. For Good has the harder job — the second act is political and considerably bleaker, and it overlaps directly with The Wizard of Oz seen from the other side.

Full details: cast and story guide

The Fantastic 4: First Steps

Pedro Pascal as Reed Richards, Vanessa Kirby as Sue Storm, with Ralph Ineson as Galactus and Julia Garner as the Silver Surfer. Directed by Matt Shakman.

Why it matters: Marvel has attempted this team three times and never landed it. Galactus being played straight rather than reduced to a cloud is the signal that this version is taking the cosmic material seriously.

Full details: cast and Doomsday connection

Also Worth Watching

  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day — Tom Holland returns. Our guide.
  • Die My Love — Jennifer Lawrence and Robert Pattinson under Lynne Ramsay. Not a blockbuster, likely the year's most punishing performance piece. Breakdown here.
  • Superman — already released, and the film DC's entire relaunch was resting on. Our breakdown.

Which Ones Actually Matter

Being honest about it, size and significance aren't the same thing.

Dune: Part Three is the one carrying the most artistic risk — it has to make audiences turn against a protagonist they've followed for two films.

Avengers: Doomsday carries the most commercial weight. Marvel's dominance has softened and this is the film expected to reverse that.

The Odyssey is the most interesting bet. An original-scale epic with no franchise attached, at a budget where failure hurts, is something almost no other director could get funded.

One caveat worth stating: release dates for films without confirmed windows move often, and studios reshuffle late in the year. Treat anything without a stated date as provisional.

Catching up before December? Our MCU watch order guide has a 14-hour shortcut, and the Loki breakdown covers the one series you can't skip.

Which one are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

For how this year is already performing at the box office, see our breakdown of the film that crossed $400 million globally.

Two more worth knowing about: The End of Oak Street, David Robert Mitchell's sci-fi thriller with Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, and Mutiny, which strands Jason Statham on a cargo ship with the people who framed him.
